23AID205 · AI, Data Science & Machine Learning project

Detecting network intrusions with the FT-Transformer

A transformer built for tabular data, compared with Logistic Regression, Random Forest and XGBoost, and with the published IDS-MTran model, on three standard intrusion-detection datasets.

1. Introduction and motivation

Every organisation connected to the internet is probed and attacked continuously: port scans, brute-force logins, exploits and, increasingly, distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) floods that use thousands of machines at once. A network intrusion detection system (NIDS) watches the traffic and raises an alarm when a flow looks malicious. Rule-based systems only catch attacks someone has already written a signature for, so machine learning is widely used to learn what attacks look like from labelled traffic.

Network traffic is usually summarised as flow records: one row per connection, with tens of numerical features (packet counts, byte rates, timing statistics, TCP flags) and a few categorical ones (protocol, service). That makes intrusion detection a tabular classification problem. Tree ensembles such as Random Forest and XGBoost are the usual strong choice for tabular data; deep models only recently became competitive. The FT-Transformer (Gorishniy et al., 2021) is one of the strongest of these: it turns every feature into a token and lets self-attention learn how features interact.

Our base paper, IDS-MTran (Xi et al., 2024), proposes a multi-scale transformer designed specifically for intrusion detection and reports over 99% accuracy on three datasets. This project asks whether a general-purpose tabular transformer, carefully evaluated, can match that, and how both compare with classical machine learning.

2. Problem statement and real-world relevance

Problem. Given a network flow record, decide whether it is normal or an attack (NSL-KDD, binary) or which type of attack it is (CIC-DDoS2019 with 12 classes, UNSW-NB15 with 10 classes), and compare how well the FT-Transformer, three classical baselines and the published IDS-MTran results solve it.

Why it matters

DDoS attacks take services offline and intrusions lead to data breaches. Detecting them early, and knowing the attack type, decides how operators respond (block a reflector, rate-limit a protocol, isolate a host).

What makes it hard

Traffic is extremely imbalanced (normal flows dominate, some attack types have only dozens of examples) and several attack types produce near-identical flow statistics.

Why careful evaluation

Public IDS datasets contain duplicates and identifier columns. If they are not handled, test rows leak into training and scores look far better than they are. We found and fixed several such issues (§4.2).

3. Objectives and scope

  1. Build a clean, leakage-free preprocessing pipeline for NSL-KDD, CIC-DDoS2019 and UNSW-NB15, using the same task as the base paper for each dataset.
  2. Explore the data: class balance, informative features, correlations and a PCA projection (dimensionality reduction).
  3. Implement and train the FT-Transformer, plus Logistic Regression, Random Forest and XGBoost baselines on identical splits.
  4. Evaluate with metrics suited to imbalanced data, repeated over 5 random seeds (mean ± standard deviation), and compare against the numbers reported for IDS-MTran.
  5. Provide a working demo that classifies new flow records with a trained model.

Scope. Offline, flow-level classification on public datasets. IDS-MTran itself is not re-implemented (no code is published and key architectural details are missing); its reported numbers are used as the reference. Live packet capture and deployment are outside the scope.

4. Methodology

4.1 Datasets

DatasetTaskWhat it containsSource
NSL-KDDbinaryCleaned version of KDD Cup '99: 41 features per connection; KDDTrain+ (125,973 rows) and KDDTest+ (22,544) Tavallaee et al. (2009); unb.ca/cic/datasets/nsl.html
CIC-DDoS201912 classesReflection/amplification DDoS attacks (DNS, LDAP, MSSQL, NTP, NetBIOS, SNMP, TFTP, UDP, UDP-Lag, Syn, WebDDoS) plus benign traffic; 77 CICFlowMeter features. We use the cleaned parquet mirror and the attack day the paper used. Sharafaldin et al. (2019); Kaggle mirror (dhoogla/cicddos2019)
UNSW-NB1510 classesFull raw release, 2.54M flows with 49 columns; normal traffic plus 9 attack categories (Analysis, Backdoor, DoS, Exploits, Fuzzers, Generic, Reconnaissance, Shellcode, Worms) Moustafa & Slay (2015); research.unsw.edu.au

The tasks match what IDS-MTran reports: binary for NSL-KDD, multi-class for the other two.

4.2 Data representation and preprocessing

Every flow is a row of numbers. Categorical columns (NSL-KDD protocol_type, service, flag; UNSW-NB15 proto, state, service) are one-hot encoded. The pipeline, in order:

  1. Drop identifiers: IP addresses, ports, timestamps, flow IDs and row IDs. They describe the lab, not the behaviour (every UNSW-NB15 attack comes from 175.45.176.0–3), so a model could "detect" attacks by address.
  2. Remove duplicate rows before splitting, so the same flow can never be in both training and test data.
  3. Stratified 70 / 15 / 15 split into train / validation / test.
  4. Impute, filter, scale using the training split only: missing values get the training median, columns constant in training are dropped, and features are standardised with a scaler fitted on training rows.

Data problems found and fixed during the project. (1) The original NSL-KDD loader merged 16 files (copies in ARFF format, subsets and a duplicated folder): 45% of test rows were also in training, inflating results. Now only KDDTrain+ and KDDTest+ are used. (2) The folder meant for CIC-DDoS2019 actually held CIC-IDS2017, a different dataset; the loader now refuses CIC-IDS2017 labels. (3) A UNSW-NB15 run used the row ID as a feature, and the files are sorted by class, so it leaked the label. (4) A mixed-type UNSW-NB15 column hid 1,371 duplicate rows. Automated tests now guard all of these (§4.8).

4.3 Exploratory data analysis and visualisation

Class balance. All three datasets are imbalanced, UNSW-NB15 extremely so: over 95% of flows are normal and the rarest attack type, Worms, has 171 rows. In CIC-DDoS2019 the WebDDoS class has only 51 rows.

Informative and correlated features. Mutual information ranks how much each feature tells us about the class. Many features are strongly correlated (for example the various SYN-error rates in NSL-KDD), which is one reason linear models struggle and attention or tree splits help.

Dimensionality reduction (PCA). Principal component analysis on a stratified sample shows how much structure a linear projection captures. In CIC-DDoS2019, DNS, LDAP, MSSQL, NetBIOS and SNMP fall on the same thin band; these reflection attacks look alike to a flow meter. In fact 3,941 CIC-DDoS2019 flows have exactly the same features as a flow with a different label, so no model can separate them perfectly.

More EDA figures

4.4 Algorithms

FT-Transformer (Feature Tokenizer + Transformer)

  1. Feature tokenizer. Each numerical feature xj becomes a 64-dimensional token xj·wj + bj. Each categorical feature becomes one learned embedding (one vector per category), so NSL-KDD is 40 tokens and UNSW-NB15 41 tokens instead of one per one-hot column.
  2. A learnable [CLS] token is prepended.
  3. 3 Transformer encoder blocks (8-head self-attention + feed-forward network, pre-layer-norm, residual connections) let every feature attend to every other.
  4. The final [CLS] representation goes through a small MLP head to class probabilities.

About 110k parameters. Unlike IDS-MTran it has no intrusion-specific design: no multi-scale convolutions, no patching. It is a general tabular model.

Baselines

  • Logistic Regression: a linear model (softmax for multi-class); shows how far a linear decision boundary gets.
  • Random Forest: 200 decision trees on bootstrap samples, averaged.
  • XGBoost: 300 gradient-boosted trees of depth 8, the usual strongest tabular baseline.

4.5 Training and validation methodology

  • Same data for every model: identical splits, preprocessing and class weights.
  • FT-Transformer: AdamW (learning rate 10-4, weight decay 10-5), batch 512, up to 100 epochs; early stopping when validation loss has not improved for 5 epochs, learning rate halved on plateaus, gradient clipping, bf16 mixed precision on an RTX 4060 laptop GPU.
  • Class imbalance: class-weighted loss for every model. Binary task: "balanced" weights, then the decision threshold is tuned on the validation split. Multi-class: square-root-balanced weights, chosen on the validation split (full balancing gave the 35 training WebDDoS rows a weight of ~500).
  • 5 seeds (42–46): each seed changes the data split and the models' random initialisation. All results are mean ± standard deviation over the 5 runs.
  • The test split is never used for any decision (thresholds, weights, early stopping all use validation data).

4.6 Evaluation metrics

  • Accuracy: share of flows classified correctly. Misleading on imbalanced data (predicting "normal" for everything scores 95.6% on UNSW-NB15).
  • Precision / recall / F1: binary: for the attack class. Multi-class: macro averages, every class counts equally, so rare attack types matter as much as common ones. Weighted F1 is reported too.
  • ROC-AUC and PR-AUC: threshold-free ranking quality (one-vs-rest per class for multi-class). PR-AUC is the more informative one for rare classes.
  • Per-class F1 and confusion matrices show which attack types are confused with which.

4.7 Compared approaches

FT-Transformer vs Logistic Regression vs Random Forest vs XGBoost, all trained here, plus the numbers reported for IDS-MTran (Xi et al., 2024; not re-trained). For IDS-MTran the paper does not state its train/test split, whether duplicates were removed, or how its multi-class precision/recall/F1 were averaged. The comparison with it is therefore indicative, while the comparison between the four models trained here is exact.

4.8 Software implementation and demo

Python 3.13, PyTorch (FT-Transformer), scikit-learn and XGBoost (baselines), pandas/NumPy (data), matplotlib (figures). The repository is organised as:

main.py                 run the full experiment for one dataset (5 seeds)
predict.py              demo: classify flow records with a trained model
src/                    config, loaders, preprocessing, FT-Transformer, training, evaluation, inference
scripts/                EDA, result charts, demo samples, this webpage
tests/                  unit tests + data validation checks
demo/                   sample flows from each test split
outputs/, checkpoints/  tables, figures, trained models

Running it:

pip install -r requirements.txt
python main.py --dataset unsw_nb15           # train + evaluate, 5 seeds
python predict.py --dataset unsw_nb15 --input demo/unsw_nb15_samples.csv
python -m unittest discover tests            # tests and validation checks

Demo. predict.py loads a trained FT-Transformer and the saved preprocessing, encodes raw flow records exactly as during training (verified automatically) and prints the predicted class and its probability. The sample flows are from each dataset's test split, so the model never saw them. Output of the UNSW-NB15 demo:

Tests and validation. tests/ checks that the splits are disjoint and stratified, that scaling and imputation use training data only, the tokenizer and model shapes, the metrics, and, on the real data, that no identifier or label column reaches the features, that no duplicate rows remain, that no test flow appears in training with the same label, and that the demo's predictions are correct.

Normal, Generic, Exploits and Reconnaissance are detected well; Analysis, Backdoor and DoS are hard for every model. These attack types are known to overlap heavily in this dataset. The FT-Transformer has the highest macro recall and the best F1 on Analysis and Backdoor, and is far ahead of Random Forest on macro F1; XGBoost is best overall.

Overall discussion

  • FT-Transformer vs classical ML. It clearly beats Logistic Regression on all three datasets and is close to the tree ensembles, ahead of Random Forest on UNSW-NB15 but slightly behind XGBoost everywhere. This matches published benchmarks: gradient-boosted trees remain hard to beat on tabular data (Grinsztajn et al., 2022).
  • Cost. The FT-Transformer needs minutes of GPU time per run, while XGBoost needs seconds to about a minute (figure below). Its advantages are flexibility (one architecture for any feature mix) and better recall on some rare classes.
  • Versus IDS-MTran. On NSL-KDD the results agree. On the multi-class datasets the paper reports ~0.99 macro-level scores, far above all four model families here, including on attack types whose flows are literally identical. With no code, split or averaging method published, we cannot explain the gap; possible factors are duplicates (the paper keeps UNSW-NB15's 2.54M raw rows; deduplication removes about three quarters of the attack rows) and a different averaging of per-class scores.
  • Accuracy hides the problem. On the multi-class datasets every model has at least 0.95 accuracy while macro F1 is only 0.44–0.72: the majority classes are easy, the rare attack types are not.
Confusion matrices and CIC-DDoS2019 per-class heatmap

6. Conclusion and future enhancements

A general-purpose tabular transformer, evaluated on leakage-free data with 5 seeds, matches the published IDS-MTran result on NSL-KDD and clearly outperforms a linear model, but gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost) remain the strongest and by far the cheapest model on all three datasets. Fine-grained multi-class detection is much harder than the near-perfect scores often reported: some attack types cannot be told apart from flow statistics alone. Careful data handling (deduplication, removing identifiers, fitting preprocessing on training data only) changed results more than the choice of model did.

Future enhancements

  • Hyperparameter search for the FT-Transformer (depth, width, learning rate), and better numerical-feature embeddings (Gorishniy et al., 2022).
  • Focal loss or hierarchical classification (first "reflection DDoS", then which protocol) for the confusable attack types.
  • Re-implement IDS-MTran and train it on the same splits for an exact comparison.
  • Generalisation tests: the official NSL-KDD test set with unseen attack types (--nsl-split official is already supported) and cross-dataset evaluation.
  • Explainability (attention maps, SHAP) and a real-time deployment on live flow data.
